name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQI_Q01 - Graph with vanishing average velocity

questiontext.text: Among the four graphs (Fig. 3.1), there is only one graph for which average velocity over the time interval \((0, T)\) can vanish for a suitably chosen \(T\). Which one is it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four position-time (\(x\)–\(t\)) graphs are given over time \(t \ge 0\). We need to identify the graph for which the average velocity over the time interval \((0, T)\) can be zero for some \(T > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Position \(x\) is plotted on the vertical axis and time \(t\) on the horizontal axis. Standard Cartesian sign conventions apply.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The average velocity over the time interval \((0, T)\) is given by: \[v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{x(T) - x(0)}{T}\] For \(v_{\text{avg}} = 0\) with \(T > 0\), the net displacement must vanish, meaning \(x(T) = x(0)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For the graph where \(x(0)\) is negative and the curve crosses the \(t\)-axis to remain positive thereafter, \(x(T) > x(0)\) for all \(T > 0\), so \(x(T) - x(0) > 0\). For the graph where \(x(0) > 0\) and \(x(t)\) decreases monotonically, \(x(T) < x(0)\) for all \(T > 0\), so \(x(T) - x(0) < 0\). For the graph where \(x(0) = 0\) and \(x(t)\) increases monotonically, \(x(T) > x(0)\) for all \(T > 0\), so \(x(T) - x(0) > 0\). For the graph where the position starts at a positive value \(x_0\) at \(t = 0\), rises to a maximum, and then decreases to values below \(x_0\), the curve must intersect the horizontal line \(x = x_0\) at some time \(T > 0\). At this time, \(x(T) = x(0)\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At the time \(T > 0\) where \(x(T) = x(0)\), the net displacement is zero, giving \(v_{\text{avg}} = 0\). Thus, the correct graph is the one that starts at a positive position \(x_0\), rises to a peak, and subsequently falls below \(x_0\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQI_Q02 - Signs of position velocity and acceleration

questiontext.text: A lift is coming from 8th floor and is just about to reach 4th floor. Taking ground floor as origin and positive direction upwards for all quantities, which one of the following is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In one-dimensional motion along a vertical axis, the signs of position \(x\), velocity \(v\), and acceleration \(a\) depend on the chosen origin and positive direction. When a moving object slows down, its acceleration is directed opposite to its velocity.

Step 2: Evaluation
The ground floor is taken as the origin (\(x = 0\)) and the upward direction is positive. The 4th floor is above the ground floor, so the position of the lift is positive (\(x > 0\)).

Step 3: Application
Since the lift is descending from the 8th floor toward the 4th floor, its direction of motion is downward, so its velocity is negative (\(v < 0\)). Because it is just about to reach the 4th floor, it is slowing down (decelerating) while moving downward. For the downward velocity to decrease in magnitude, the acceleration must act in the upward direction, making it positive (\(a > 0\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(x > 0\), \(v < 0\), and \(a > 0\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQI_Q03 - Bounds on displacement from speed

questiontext.text: In one dimensional motion, instantaneous speed \(v\) satisfies \(0 \le v < v_0\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
For a particle in one-dimensional motion, the instantaneous speed \(v\) satisfies \(0 \le v < v_0\) over a time interval \(T > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the one-dimensional motion take place along the \(x\)-axis, with instantaneous velocity \(v_x = \frac{dx}{dt}\) and instantaneous speed \(v = |v_x|\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Since \(|v_x| < v_0\), the instantaneous velocity is bounded by: \[-v_0 < v_x < v_0\] The displacement \(x\) in time \(T\) is given by: \[x = \int_0^T v_x \, dt\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Integrating the velocity bounds from \(t = 0\) to \(t = T\): \[\int_0^T (-v_0) \, dt < \int_0^T v_x \, dt < \int_0^T v_0 \, dt\] \[-v_0 T < x < v_0 T\] Notice that displacement can be negative if \(v_x < 0\), acceleration can be positive, negative, or zero, and turning points can exist wherever \(v = 0\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The bounds \(-v_0 T < x < v_0 T\) have units of length and hold for any motion with speed strictly less than \(v_0\). Thus, the displacement \(x\) in time \(T\) satisfies \(-v_0 T < x < v_0 T\).

answer.text: The displacement in time \(T\) must always take non-negative values.
The displacement \(x\) in time \(T\) satisfies \(-v_0 T < x < v_0 T\).
The acceleration is always a non-negative number.

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQI_Q04 - Average speed over equal half distances

questiontext.text: A vehicle travels half the distance \(L\) with speed \(V_1\) and the other half with speed \(V_2\), then its average speed is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total distance travelled \(= L\). First half distance \(= \frac{L}{2}\) is travelled with speed \(V_1\). Second half distance \(= \frac{L}{2}\) is travelled with speed \(V_2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both speeds \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) are positive and constant over their respective halves of the journey.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average speed is defined as the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken: \[v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Time taken for the first half: \[t_1 = \frac{L/2}{V_1} = \frac{L}{2V_1}\] Time taken for the second half: \[t_2 = \frac{L/2}{V_2} = \frac{L}{2V_2}\] Total time taken: \[T = t_1 + t_2 = \frac{L}{2}\left(\frac{1}{V_1} + \frac{1}{V_2}\right) = \frac{L(V_1 + V_2)}{2V_1V_2}\] Therefore, the average speed is: \[v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{L}{T} = \frac{L}{\frac{L(V_1 + V_2)}{2V_1V_2}} = \frac{2V_1V_2}{V_1 + V_2}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
If \(V_1 = V_2 = V\), the formula gives \(\frac{2V^2}{2V} = V\), which is physically consistent. Thus, the average speed is \(\frac{2V_1V_2}{V_1 + V_2}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQI_Q05 - Distance covered with turning point

questiontext.text: The displacement of a particle is given by \(x = (t - 2)^2\) where \(x\) is in metres and \(t\) in seconds. The distance covered by the particle in first 4 seconds is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position of the particle as a function of time is \(x(t) = (t - 2)^2\text{ m}\), for the time interval \(t = 0\) to \(t = 4\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is along the \(x\)-axis. Distance is a non-negative scalar representing the total path length, whereas displacement can change sign if the particle reverses direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Instantaneous velocity is \(v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}\). Turning points occur where \(v(t) = 0\). Total distance over \([0, 4]\) is obtained by summing the magnitudes of displacements between turning points.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating \(x(t)\) with respect to \(t\): \[v(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(t - 2)^2 = 2(t - 2)\text{ m/s}\] Setting \(v(t) = 0\) gives \(t = 2\text{ s}\), which lies in the interval \([0, 4]\text{ s}\). Evaluating the positions at \(t = 0\), \(t = 2\text{ s}\), and \(t = 4\text{ s}\): \[x(0) = (0 - 2)^2 = 4\text{ m}\] \[x(2) = (2 - 2)^2 = 0\text{ m}\] \[x(4) = (4 - 2)^2 = 4\text{ m}\] Distance covered from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 2\text{ s}\): \[d_1 = |x(2) - x(0)| = |0 - 4| = 4\text{ m}\] Distance covered from \(t = 2\text{ s}\) to \(t = 4\text{ s}\): \[d_2 = |x(4) - x(2)| = |4 - 0| = 4\text{ m}\] Total distance covered: \[d = d_1 + d_2 = 4\text{ m} + 4\text{ m} = 8\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Although the net displacement \(x(4) - x(0) = 0\), the particle moves \(4\text{ m}\) to the origin and \(4\text{ m}\) back, giving a total distance of \(8\text{ m}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQI_Q06 - Walking up a moving escalator

questiontext.text: At a metro station, a girl walks up a stationary escalator in time \(t_1\). If she remains stationary on the escalator, then the escalator take her up in time \(t_2\). The time taken by her to walk up on the moving escalator will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Time taken by the girl to walk up the stationary escalator \(= t_1\). Time taken by the moving escalator to carry the stationary girl up \(= t_2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the length of the escalator be \(L\). Both the girl's walking speed relative to the escalator and the escalator's speed relative to the ground are constant and directed upward.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
When the girl walks up on the moving escalator, her speed relative to the ground is the sum of her walking speed relative to the escalator and the escalator's speed relative to the ground: \[v_{\text{net}} = v_{\text{girl}} + v_{\text{escalator}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Speed of the girl relative to the escalator: \[v_{\text{girl}} = \frac{L}{t_1}\] Speed of the escalator relative to the ground: \[v_{\text{escalator}} = \frac{L}{t_2}\] Net upward speed relative to the ground: \[v_{\text{net}} = \frac{L}{t_1} + \frac{L}{t_2} = L\left(\frac{t_1 + t_2}{t_1 t_2}\right)\] Time \(t\) taken to cover distance \(L\) on the moving escalator: \[t = \frac{L}{v_{\text{net}}} = \frac{L}{L\left(\frac{t_1 + t_2}{t_1 t_2}\right)} = \frac{t_1 t_2}{t_2 + t_1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The expression \(\frac{t_1 t_2}{t_2 + t_1}\) has dimensions of time and is smaller than both \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), as expected. Thus, the time taken is \(\frac{t_1 t_2}{t_2 + t_1}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQII_Q07 - Linear graph of motion quantities

questiontext.text: The variation of quantity \(A\) with quantity \(B\), plotted in Fig. 3.2 describes the motion of a particle in a straight line.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The plot of quantity \(A\) (vertical axis) versus quantity \(B\) (horizontal axis) is a straight line with a positive \(A\)-intercept and a positive constant slope, represented by \(A = A_0 + mB\) with \(A_0 > 0\) and \(m > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Straight-line motion is described by standard kinematic relations between displacement \(x\), velocity \(v\), acceleration \(a\), and time \(t\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. For uniform motion (\(a = 0\)): \(v = \text{constant}\), and \(x = x_0 + vt\). 2. For uniformly accelerated motion (\(a = \text{constant} \ne 0\)): \(v = v_0 + at\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
If quantity \(B\) represents time \(t\), then: - When the motion is uniform, \(x = x_0 + vt\) has the linear form \(A = A_0 + mB\), so quantity \(A\) can represent displacement. - When the motion is uniform, velocity \(v\) is constant, which would be a horizontal line rather than a line with positive slope, so quantity \(A\) cannot be velocity for uniform motion. - When the motion is uniformly accelerated, \(v = v_0 + at\) has the linear form \(A = A_0 + mB\), so quantity \(A\) can represent velocity.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Hence, quantity \(B\) may represent time, quantity \(A\) is displacement if motion is uniform, and quantity \(A\) is velocity if motion is uniformly accelerated.

answer.text: Quantity \(A\) is velocity if motion is uniform.
Quantity \(A\) is displacement if motion is uniform.
Quantity \(A\) is velocity if motion is uniformly accelerated.

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQII_Q08 - Interpreting position versus time graph

questiontext.text: A graph of \(x\) versus \(t\) is shown in Fig. 3.3. Choose correct alternatives from below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A position-time (\(x\)–\(t\)) graph is given with marked points A (at \(t = 0\)), B (local maximum), C (horizontal point of inflection), D (crossing the \(t\)-axis), and E (on the rising branch near the top).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the \(x\)–\(t\) graph, \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\), and acceleration is determined by the concavity, \(a = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- \(v = 0\) where the tangent is horizontal. - \(a > 0\) where the graph is concave upward; \(a < 0\) where the graph is concave downward; \(a = 0\) at an inflection point. - Average velocity between two points is \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}\). - Speed is \(|v| = \left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- At \(t = 0\) (point A), the tangent to the curve is horizontal, so \(v = 0\); thus, the particle was released from rest at \(t = 0\). - At B, the curve has a local maximum and is concave downward, so \(a < 0\) (not \(a > 0\)). - At C, the curve has a horizontal tangent (\(v = 0\)) and changes concavity from upward to downward (point of inflection, \(a = 0\)), so both velocity and acceleration vanish. - Between A and D, \(x_D = 0\) while \(x_A > 0\), so \(x_D - x_A < 0\) and the average velocity is negative (not positive). - Comparing slopes, the curve is much steeper at D than at E, so \(\left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|_D > \left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|_E\), meaning the speed at D exceeds that at E.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the correct statements are that the particle was released from rest at \(t = 0\), both velocity and acceleration vanish at C, and the speed at D exceeds that at E.

answer.text: The particle was released from rest at \(t = 0\).
At C, the velocity and the acceleration vanish.
Average velocity for the motion between A and D is positive.
The speed at D exceeds that at E.

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQII_Q09 - Kinematics of sinusoidal one dimensional motion

questiontext.text: For the one-dimensional motion, described by \(x = t - \sin t\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position as a function of time is \(x(t) = t - \sin t\) for \(t > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Time \(t\) is in radians for the trigonometric function, and standard calculus definitions of velocity and acceleration apply.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}, \quad a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For all \(t > 0\), \(\sin t < t\), so \(x(t) = t - \sin t > 0\) for all \(t > 0\). 2. Differentiating \(x(t)\) gives the velocity: \[v(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(t - \sin t) = 1 - \cos t\] Since \(-1 \le \cos t \le 1\), we have \(0 \le 1 - \cos t \le 2\), so \(v(t)\) lies between \(0\) and \(2\). However, \(v(t) = 0\) whenever \(\cos t = 1\) (e.g., at \(t = 2\pi\)), so \(v(t)\) is not strictly greater than \(0\) for all \(t > 0\). 3. Differentiating \(v(t)\) gives the acceleration: \[a(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(1 - \cos t) = \sin t\] Since \(\sin t\) takes negative values (for example, in the interval \(\pi < t < 2\pi\)), \(a(t)\) is not positive for all \(t > 0\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, \(x(t) > 0\) for all \(t > 0\) and \(v(t)\) lies between \(0\) and \(2\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQII_Q10 - Acceleration and speed of oscillating spring mass

questiontext.text: A spring with one end attached to a mass and the other to a rigid support is stretched and released.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A mass attached to a spring stretched and released undergoes simple harmonic motion (SHM) about its equilibrium position \(x = 0\) with amplitude \(A\).

Step 2: Evaluation
In SHM, the magnitude of acceleration is \(|a| = \omega^2 |x|\), and the speed is \(v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}\), where \(\omega\) is the angular frequency and \(x\) is the displacement from equilibrium.

Step 3: Application
- When the mass is just released, \(|x| = A\) is maximum, so the magnitude of acceleration \(|a| = \omega^2 A\) is maximum. - At the equilibrium position (\(x = 0\)), the acceleration is zero (minimum), while the speed \(v = \omega A\) is maximum. - Whenever the speed is minimum (\(v = 0\)), we have \(A^2 - x^2 = 0\), so \(|x| = A\), meaning the magnitude of displacement is maximum.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the magnitude of acceleration is maximum when just released, the speed is maximum at the equilibrium position, and the magnitude of displacement is always maximum whenever speed is minimum.

answer.text: Magnitude of acceleration, when just released is maximum.
Magnitude of acceleration, when at equilibrium position, is maximum.
Speed is maximum when mass is at equilibrium position.
Magnitude of displacement is always maximum whenever speed is minimum.

name.text: PHYSICS_MOTIONINASTRAIGHTLINE_MCQII_Q11 - Elastic bouncing ball inside moving train

questiontext.text: A ball is bouncing elastically with a speed \(1\text{ m/s}\) between walls of a railway compartment of size \(10\text{ m}\) in a direction perpendicular to walls. The train is moving at a constant velocity of \(10\text{ m/s}\) parallel to the direction of motion of the ball. As seen from the ground,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Speed of the ball relative to the train compartment \(= 1\text{ m/s}\). Distance between the walls \(= 10\text{ m}\). Constant velocity of the train relative to the ground \(= +10\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Take the direction of the train's motion as positive. Since the train moves at constant velocity, it forms an inertial reference frame.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Galilean velocity transformation: \[v_{\text{ball, ground}} = v_{\text{ball, train}} + v_{\text{train, ground}}\] Since \(v_{\text{train, ground}}\) is constant, acceleration is invariant: \[a_{\text{ball, ground}} = a_{\text{ball, train}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In the train's frame, the time between consecutive wall collisions is: \[\Delta t = \frac{10\text{ m}}{1\text{ m/s}} = 10\text{ s}\] As seen from the ground: - When the ball moves in the direction of the train, its velocity is \(10 + 1 = +11\text{ m/s}\). - When the ball moves opposite to the train (in the train's frame), its velocity relative to the ground is \(10 - 1 = +9\text{ m/s}\). Both velocities are positive, so the direction of motion of the ball relative to the ground never changes. However, its speed alternates between \(11\text{ m/s}\) and \(9\text{ m/s}\) every \(10\text{ s}\). Over any \(20\text{ s}\) interval (one complete back-and-forth period), the ball spends \(10\text{ s}\) at \(11\text{ m/s}\) and \(10\text{ s}\) at \(9\text{ m/s}\), so the total distance is \(11(10) + 9(10) = 200\text{ m}\), giving a fixed average speed of \(\frac{200\text{ m}}{20\text{ s}} = 10\text{ m/s}\). Because the train moves with constant velocity, the acceleration of the ball as seen from the ground is identical to that seen from the train.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, as seen from the ground, the speed of the ball changes every 10 seconds, the average speed over any 20 second interval is fixed, and the acceleration is the same as from the train.

answer.text: the direction of motion of the ball changes every 10 seconds.
average speed of ball over any 20 second interval is fixed.
the acceleration of ball is the same as from the train.
